a6189.speech: Said BAP would help the private sector navigate complexities of the business landscape and support the health care business among others; also encouraged the private sector to embrace Artificial Intelligence to avoid their businesses being left behind.

a6206.speaker: Study by the National Planning Commission (NPC) and the International Food Policy Research Institute (Ifpri)
a6206.speech: Shows that as of March 2025, two months after the US halted funding to Malawi and other countries, at least 4,451 healthcare staff relying on US funding had their contracts terminated, and found that the donor cut affected health service delivery in the country ; Found that even though key health programmes such as those related to HIV and Aids and malaria management appear to be subject to more modest cuts, several health-related services have been interrupted or are operating at reduced capacity ; “As of March, 4 451 health staff reliant on US funding had had their contracts terminated and 18 drop-in centres serving populations living with HIV had closed down [UNAids, 2025]. More broadly, cuts to treatment and prevention activities, including for example vaccination efforts supported by Global Vaccine Alliance [Gavi], will aggravate the spread of many infectious diseases leading to loss of lives and quality of life.”

a6206.speaker: Study by the National Planning Commission (NPC) and the International Food Policy Research Institute (Ifpri)
a6206.speech: Recommends that government must evaluate the vulnerability of crucial services to aid cuts and collaborate with development partners to identify those whose loss would have the most severe impact: “Funding sources for the most essential programme should be diversified to reduce reliance on any single donor, which can jeopardise service continuity. In the current environment where traditional bilateral donors are reducing their development assistance budgets, a more balanced approach is needed.”

a6206.speaker: Thom Khanje, NPC public relations and communications manager
a6206.speech: Confirmed that by March this year 4 451 health staff relying on US funding had their contracts terminated: “Yes, [the figure] it’s correct.”

a6206.speaker: George Jobe, Malawi Health Equity Network executive director
a6206.speech: Expressed worry that many health personnel are now jobless following the US aid freeze.

a6725.speaker: Physicians for Human Rights (PHR) report
a6725.speech: Recently released a report on the crisis that the Donald Trump administration's cutting off of the humanitarian aid the United States had long provided to developing countries is causing in the health sector of countries such as Ethiopia; the report says that merely because programmes such as PEPFAR were suspended for 90 days, up to 100,000 additional people worldwide and up to 3,600 in Ethiopia could face the risk of death from HIV/AIDS and related health problems.

a6725.speaker: Ahmed Shide, Ethiopian Minister of Finance
a6725.speech: Had said that the sharp decline in the support that some countries he described as development partners channel to Ethiopia in the health sector has challenged the sector; explained that even if these countries intended to resume their interrupted support, the government has put forward as a solution a plan to cover the bulk of the sector's budget from its own resources so that the sector does not face a similar budget shortfall.

a6725.speaker: Members of the Ethiopian House of People's Representatives
a6725.speech: Repeatedly asked whether there was any planned salary and benefit increase for health professionals, as well as for teachers and other government employees on whom the cost of living weighs heavily; raised strong questions that the inflation figure released by the Ethiopian Statistical Service does not reflect the actual price increases and cost-of-living burden citizens face, and that society is embittered by overlapping tax burdens; and asked that, while reports on waste in budget use and audit shortcomings indicate a concrete problem, the government's planning of an ever-growing budget each year for budget-holding institutions and the regions is harming the country and should be reconsidered.

a6725.speaker: Draft 2018 (Ethiopian calendar) budget report of the Ministry of Finance
a6725.speech: “As the national economic accounts data show, the Ethiopian economy recorded an average annual growth of 7.2 percent in the years from 2010 to 2016, while in the 2016 fiscal year it had a higher growth of 8.1 percent” ; the report also states that inflation has fluctuated in double digits since reaching an average of about 14 percent in 2009, reaching up to 35 percent; that the birr's purchasing power against the dollar declined by an average of 13 percent between 2009 and 2016; that government expenditure grew by 19 percent between 2009 and 2016 (recurrent 21 percent, capital only 18 percent); and that debt-repayment pressure is competing with the capital budget, development spending and poverty-reduction work.

a6725.speaker: Bulcha Demeksa, late former member of the Ethiopian parliament
a6725.speech: “To grow by 11 percent is a miracle. Those who performed this miracle are the likes of China, Taiwan and South Korea. But how do we say we grew by 11 percent? Countries like Angola that suddenly found oil are growing by 12 percent. Institutions like the IMF have said that countries like Ethiopia will grow by six percent even this year. But we refuse and say we grew by 11 percent. And how are we going to explain this to the world?”

a6725.speaker: Ahmed Shide, Ethiopian Minister of Finance
a6725.speech: Repeatedly raised the debt question, saying, “We are paying a legacy of debt burden” ; noted that the payments on debts taken on by the previous government rather than the current one are high, stating that debt interest payments grew from eight billion birr in 2009 to 68 billion birr in 2016 ; was heard saying, “Obtaining a one-year grace period on debt repayment has benefited us greatly”, and indicated he is in a process of discussion, in which understanding has been reached with organisations such as the IMF, on a 3.5 billion dollar debt restructuring expected to produce results soon.

a6725.speaker: Ahmed Shide, Ethiopian Minister of Finance
a6725.speech: Stated that the budget as planned has a gross deficit of 417 billion birr relative to revenue, and indicated a plan to cover 139 billion birr from abroad through aid and loans and 278 billion birr from the domestic budget; repeatedly mentioned that his government obtained all of these economic results by carrying out effective economic reform.

a6725.speaker: Government of Ethiopia
a6725.speech: Stated that it prepared the 2018 budget on the assumption of a total of 1.5 trillion birr in revenue from domestic sources and from abroad in aid and loans, and indicated that the draft presents a total budget of 1.95 trillion birr for recurrent spending, capital spending, support to the regions and reinforcement of the sustainable development goals; said it is still continuing to subsidise basic supplies such as fuel and fertiliser in order to ease the cost-of-living pressure on citizens.

a6725.speaker: Getachew Paulos, economist (interviewed by Reporter)
a6725.speech: Began with the question, “Does the Ethiopian economy have the capacity to carry this entire budget?” and explained: “First, the plan is indicative that there may be an intention to raise the price of foreign exchange transactions. One can guess that the birr's purchasing power against the dollar will weaken even further than it is now. From which industry, from which trader and taxpayer are they going to collect all this birr? The budget appears very impulsive and stretched. It signals that society should prepare for greater cost of living and cost-of-living pressure. The strategies and tax practices the government follows in order to raise its revenue are largely not knowledge-based and not citizen-focused... In my estimation the Ethiopian economy will not carry a two trillion birr budget. The budget plan is one that greatly distresses and puts pressure on the government itself, while for citizens it may have the effect of bringing about a bitter cost-of-living burden.”

a6725.speaker: Getachew Paulos, economist (interviewed by Reporter)
a6725.speech: “Both the trader and the public must prepare themselves. Everyone must strive as much as possible to create additional sources of income. That the economy is slowing is a visible fact. The government, meanwhile, has focused broadly on urban development projects... Last year they planned a budget of one trillion. This year they have presented two trillion, double that. By their own admission the economy grew by eight percent in one year, not double. Today the price of fertiliser has doubled and it was distributed at more than seven thousand birr per quintal. At what price is the farmer going to sell what he produced after bearing the cost of fertiliser and other things?... Given the stretched budget presented this year, an increase in this kind of tax dispute is to be expected.”

a6725.speaker: Desalegn Chane (PhD), parliamentary representative of the National Movement of Amhara (NAMA)
a6725.speech: Criticised as “a game” the draft budget's presentation that “the value-added tax and excise tax collected from fuel will be used to subsidise citizens' living”, noting that saying citizens' living is being subsidised by imposing additional taxes, when it would be possible to subsidise them by not imposing those taxes, is untenable.

a6725.speaker: Kristalina Georgieva, Managing Director of the International Monetary Fund (IMF)
a6725.speech: “Transforming an economy is not like sipping coffee while it is hot; it takes time. It requires the government's political commitment. And equally, it requires the support of all Ethiopians” ; “Ethiopians, you are a people who made Africa proud by winning the victory of Adwa, and I have no doubt that today too you will show the world your heroism again through the success of economic reform” ; “We have no doubt that your future will be bright, so push on with your reform” ; set out prominently that opening the economy wide to the private sector, expanding new business opportunities and broadly seeking revenue alternatives are key matters; and told Finance Minister Ahmed that “you are successfully carrying out the economic reform”, bestowing hope that if Ethiopia runs the reform in this way it will be successful.

a6725.speaker: Ahmed Shide, Ethiopian Minister of Finance
a6725.speech: “The main objective of the foreign exchange market reform is to create a modern and effective foreign exchange market, to resolve macroeconomic distortions, to bring multi-sector growth and to increase the role of the private sector” ; citing average growth of six percent from 2012 to 2015 and about eight percent in 2016, indicated this will continue this year; promised that the growth path the country has taken is the correct one and that the cost-of-living pressure citizens face will be eased within a few years.

a6725.speaker: Abiy Ahmed (PhD), Prime Minister of Ethiopia
a6725.speech: In an extensive interview with the national television station said, “Ethiopia is in an era of revival”, pointing out that the economy is recovering after withstanding the challenges it faced, stating that if it continues this way for the next five or even ten years the country will be transformed, and asking the Ethiopian people to receive the coming change with patience.

a6927.speaker: Richard Mills Jr, US Ambassador to Nigeria
a6927.speech: Has said that there's no evidence to back allegations that USAID funded the Boko Haram terrorist group in the country, that his government monitors all its spending in Nigeria and none of that went to Boko Haram, and that robust monitoring systems were in place to ensure US assistance reached the intended recipients; he challenged anyone with evidence of misappropriation to present it, saying it would be thoroughly investigated in collaboration with Nigerian partners: "There's no friend of Nigeria that has been stronger in its condemnation of the violence of Boko Haram and Boko Haram's contempt for human life than the United States. We labelled Boko Haram since 2013 a foreign terrorist organisation, a designation that was designed to block Boko Haram from carrying out any asset transfers to the United States. This allows us to arrest and seize members of Boko Haram and allows us to cooperate in investigations with the Nigerian government. I can assure you, we have policies and procedures in place to ensure that USAID funding, any of our assistance funding, whether that comes from USAID, the Department of Defense, is not diverted to a terrorist group like Boko Haram. There is absolutely no evidence that I have seen that has occurred. And certainly if we ever had evidence presented to us that a programme funding was being diverted to Boko Haram, we would immediately investigate along with our Nigerian partners. I just want to be clear that when it comes to Boko Haram, the United States stands with Nigeria in wanting to rid this country of the scourge that the organisation represents."

a6927.speaker: Scott Perry, US Congressman (Republican)
a6927.speech: Recently claimed that the USAID funded global terrorist groups like Boko Haram, although he provided no evidence of his claim.

a6927.speaker: Richard Mills Jr, US Ambassador to Nigeria
a6927.speech: Clarified that the US had not cut its financial aid to Nigeria, but put in a 90-day pause: "In fact, the US Secretary of State, Marco Rubio said this is not about ending foreign assistance to our partners and friends like Nigeria. It's about how to make the assistance more effective and how to make sure that it aligns with US government policies and interests. So that's what this 90-day pause is for in our assistance. But I think many of you have seen, I hope, that there are waivers. Waivers for our assistance that's life-saving, that provides humanitarian, life-saving assistance, whether that's to HIV patients or to mother and child nutrition needs, to internally displaced people."

a6927.speaker: Marco Rubio, US Secretary of State (quoted by Ambassador Mills)
a6927.speech: "This is not about ending foreign assistance to our partners and friends like Nigeria. It's about how to make the assistance more effective and how to make sure that it aligns with US government policies and interests."

a6927.speaker: Richard Mills Jr, US Ambassador to Nigeria
a6927.speech: Said that in his presentation to the Nigerian Governors' Forum he highlighted his vision on the US-Nigeria relationship over the next four years, focusing on four key priorities, which he listed as promoting more investment, transparency and accountability; combating corruption and empowering local authorities; and advocating for transparency in Nigeria; adding that the US wanted to be more engaged at the sub-national level, at the state and local governing authorities, as it develops its programmes and assistance for Nigeria.

a6927.speaker: Richard Mills Jr, US Ambassador to Nigeria
a6927.speech: Said he also discussed the transition of healthcare programmes in Nigeria that were being supported by the US: "As those programmes are succeeding, as less people have HIV, as polio vaccinations have helped eradicate polio, we want to start transitioning those programmes. So, how do we keep our health programmes sustainable and transfer them to the Nigerian government so they can run them and make them more effective? We'd like to help develop capacity, the capacity of the states, and the local governing authorities. I think this is partly driven by the Supreme Court decision last summer that is going to give the LGAs, if this unfolds the way we think it will, perhaps some authority, more fiscal responsibility. We want to help the LGAs transition, take on this new responsibility, and make sure they can work well with the states, based on our experience in the US, where we have a federal system too, where one of our governing principles is, the most effective government is government close to the people."

a6938.speaker: Carla Louveira, Mozambican Finance Minister
a6938.speech: Has recognised that health care will be the sector most affected by the suspension of foreign aid by the United States under the Trump administration; expressed concern at the suspension of US funding for health programmes, particularly in the area of HIV/AIDS, endangering HIV tests and counselling, the treatment of HIV and tuberculosis, and the prevention of the transmission of HIV from pregnant women to their unborn children; warned that the suspension of American aid "presents a significant challenge for the health sector, directly affecting the provision of essential health services and the sustainability of priority and strategic programmes"; and lamented that suspension of the US aid threatens the lives of millions of Mozambicans, particularly because it is not known how long the suspension will last, bearing in mind that there are no resources in the 2025 Mozambican state budget to cope with the suspension.

a6938.speaker: Carla Louveira, Mozambican Finance Minister
a6938.speech: Declared, as cited by the independent newsheet "Mediafax", that the Mozambican government is willing to deepen still further what are still called "links of cooperation and friendship" with the United States through partnerships in various areas.

a6938.speaker: Vrooman, US Ambassador to Mozambique
a6938.speech: Guaranteed that US assistance through PEPFAR will continue, thus ensuring ongoing prevention of HIV infections, including mother-to-child HIV transmission.

a6938.speaker: Mediafax (independent newsheet)
a6938.speech: Cited as the source for the Finance Minister's declaration that the Mozambican government is willing to deepen its "links of cooperation and friendship" with the United States through partnerships in various areas.

a6964.speaker: Nozipho Mlotshwa, 32, South African lab technician, Antiviral Gene Therapy Research Unit, University of the Witwatersrand
a6964.speech: "This was very exciting. We were getting quite good results," Mlotshwa told Reuters in the lab.

a6964.speaker: U.S. State Department
a6964.speech: Did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

a6964.speaker: Nigel Garrett, Chief Scientific Officer at the Desmond Tutu Health Foundation
a6964.speech: "It feels like you're building something and you could really make a huge difference. And then it's wiped away."

a6964.speaker: Patrick Arbuthnot, director of the Antiviral Gene Therapy Research Unit
a6964.speech: "We were gaining momentum," said Arbuthnot, adding: "an HIV vaccine is the holy grail of the field".

a6964.speaker: U.S. President Donald Trump (executive orders)
a6964.speech: Ordered in January a 90-day pause in all foreign development assistance pending assessment of its consistency with his "America First" foreign policy; separately targeted South Africa with an executive order to cut all funding to the country, citing disapproval of its land reform policy and its genocide case against U.S. ally Israel.

a6964.speaker: Ntobeko Ntusi, CEO of the South African Medical Research Council
a6964.speech: "Most of the landmark and groundbreaking studies have been conducted in this country. But these have been good for the whole world."

a6964.speaker: Ntobeko Ntusi, CEO of the South African Medical Research Council
a6964.speech: Said he did not expect funding for projects like BRILLIANT to resume, given the executive order on aid to South Africa; said the council gets about a third of its funding from U.S. federal sources, for research that is mostly on HIV and tuberculosis but covers other areas including maternal and infant mortality and antimicrobial resistance.

a6964.speaker: Nigel Garrett, Chief Scientific Officer at the Desmond Tutu Health Foundation
a6964.speech: Said the shot that was ready for testing on humans was a mix of two vaccine substances developed in the United States and the Netherlands which have shown promise but never been tested together, and that they are now sitting in storage. "We had a huge opportunity, good funding. It's difficult for other funders to fill that gap."

a7083.speaker: Dambisa Moyo, author of Dead Aid
a7083.speech: Discusses why aid does not really work in most African countries that are dependent on the West for survival; views the aid that comes to these countries as harmful because it perpetuates corruption and dependency, rather than promoting sustainable development and economic growth; observes that more than 50 years of aid from the West has not significantly developed Africa.

a7083.speaker: Donald Trump, United States President
a7083.speech: Echoed Moyo's sentiments, having frozen aid provided through the US Agency for International Development (USaid), and threatened to completely shut down USaid.

a7083.speaker: Government of Malawi
a7083.speech: Has said that it is looking for alternatives to USaid.

a7353.speaker: Hajime Kimura, Japanese Ambassador to Mozambique
a7353.speech: declared at the signing ceremony in Maputo on Wednesday: “We shall continue to support the struggle of Mozambique against insecurity and also against the pandemic. Japan will always be at your side”.

a7353.speaker: United Nations (estimates)
a7353.speech: United Nations estimates indicate that 1.3 million people are in urgent need of humanitarian assistance in Cabo Delgado and in the neighbouring provinces of Nampula and Niassa because of the Covid-19 pandemic and the terrorist attacks.

a7353.speaker: Myrta Kaulard, Resident Coordinator of the UN system in Mozambique
a7353.speech: “The generous contribution by Japan will save the lives of tens of thousands of people who have fled from armed violence in the far north of Mozambique, losing all that they owned” ; “It will also support the tens of thousands who are sharing the little they have to welcome those who have fled” ; “This is a great demonstration of solidarity and of the value of multilateralism” ; “I hope that many others will follow this example to attend to the urgent humanitarian needs in northern Mozambique”.

a7353.speaker: Cesar Tembo, representative of the Mozambican government’s relief agency, the National Disaster Management and Risk Reduction Institute (IND)
a7353.speech: recognised that the challenges are enormous. He said that about 660,000 displaced people have been registered, of whom 345,000 are children ; “The humanitarian assistance needs are multiform and require permanent interventions”.

a7422.speaker: Sean Jones, USAID Ethiopia Mission Director
a7422.speech: “These elections belong to the Ethiopian people, and we are proud to be welcomed as a partner in supporting free and fair elections, and ensuring that the voices of Ethiopians in every corner of the country are heard as this country continues its remarkable journey.”

a7431.speaker: Mike Childs, head of policy at Friends of the Earth
a7431.speech: “If the UK suffered tens of billions of pounds worth of damage caused by other countries’ actions, our government and the public would rightfully be shouting from the rooftops about the injustice” ; “Yet this is the reality for many countries on the front lines of climate breakdown that have contributed virtually nothing to global emissions.”

a7431.speaker: Carla Denyer, co-leader of the Green Party
a7431.speech: “It’s deeply unjust that those who have done the least to contribute to the climate crisis are paying most dearly for it – the UK has a central role to play in righting that injustice” ; “While governments like ours delay, countries like Somalia and Ethiopia, and small island nations – some of the world’s poorest countries – are paying the price” ; “The government’s recent cuts to the foreign aid budget are particularly disturbing in this context, with so many across the world relying on essential humanitarian aid as a result of extreme weather caused by the climate crisis.”

a7431.speaker: Emily Wilkinson, principal research fellow at ODI Global
a7431.speech: “Every year, we see more devastation from the worsening effects of climate change” ; “Wealthier nations urgently need to scale up climate finance and also make sure it reaches the right places. For remote or unstable places [facing conflict or other vulnerabilities], such as those featured in the study, getting projects off the ground might be harder, but the benefits will also be more keenly felt by affected populations.”

a7431.speaker: Emily Wilkinson, research fellow at ODI Global
a7431.speech: “The escalating costs from climate change will have a serious toll on economic growth and living standards, and a wider risk of geopolitical stability in some regions” ; “Climate change contributing to a poorer, more dangerous, future is bad for everyone, but we are not too late to change course.”

a7431.speaker: ODI Global report / researchers (study of 53 low-income countries)
a7431.speech: Found that since the year 2000 these countries have suffered $395bn in losses and damages from extreme weather events, $156bn of which can be attributed to the climate crisis; that climate change contributed to at least $11.5bn in losses and damages to livestock and crops in the Sahel and Horn of Africa; that Somalia has suffered the worst of all, with $151bn in losses and damages, $75bn of which is estimated attributable to climate change; researchers found Somalia’s extended droughts have been exacerbated by the climate crisis, contributing to lower rainfall, warmer air temperatures and higher evapotranspiration ; ODI Global’s researchers warn these effects will only continue to get worse and estimate at least a further $235bn in these countries from climate-related damages if the planet warms by 2C compared to pre-industrial levels. The research uses climate mapping studies combined with figures from EM-DAT, the international database covering mass disasters worldwide, and United Nations disaster reports.

a7431.speaker: Climate scientists at Europe’s Copernicus Climate Change Service (C3S)
a7431.speech: According to climate scientists at C3S, each of the past 10 years (2015–2024) was one of the 10 warmest years on record, and the monthly global average temperature exceeded 1.5C above pre-industrial levels for 11 months of the year.

a7431.speaker: International Development Committee
a7431.speech: Reported that just this week the UK government refused to reconsider its cuts to aid spending and could not commit to funding for nutrition.

a7431.speaker: Spokesperson for the Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office
a7431.speech: “Demands for action from the world’s most vulnerable and the requirements for delivering security for British citizens are fundamentally aligned. That is why we are supporting those who are experiencing the worst impacts of the climate crisis and working together with partners to meet the objectives of the Paris Agreement.”

a7431.speaker: Charities
a7431.speech: Are worried that aid cuts will limit their ability to respond to food shortages as Somalia faces drought and low crop yields once again.
